clinicalPearls: A vision-threatening consequence of chronic ocular hypoperfusion, usually from severe (often more than 90 percent) ipsilateral carotid occlusive disease
Typically affects older patients with widespread atherosclerosis and shares risk factors with stroke and coronary disease
Symptoms include gradual or sudden visual loss, a dull ocular or periorbital ache, and prolonged recovery of vision after exposure to bright light

Anterior segment signs include episcleral congestion, a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil, iris and angle neovascularisation (rubeosis) and, in some, flare and low intraocular pressure from reduced aqueous production
Posterior segment shows narrowed arteries, dilated but not tortuous veins, mid-peripheral dot-and-blot haemorrhages and, in some, spontaneous arterial pulsation on gentle globe pressure
Fluorescein angiography reveals delayed arm-to-retina and prolonged arteriovenous transit times and patchy choroidal filling
It is both a sight-threatening and a life-threatening condition, mandating carotid imaging and vascular risk management to reduce stroke and cardiac mortality
Management principles combine treatment of the carotid disease and systemic risk factors with panretinal photocoagulation and anti-VEGF for neovascularisation and control of neovascular glaucoma
reference.pathophysiology: Ocular ischaemic syndrome results from chronic hypoperfusion of the eye, most often due to severe stenosis or occlusion of the ipsilateral internal or common carotid artery, and less commonly ophthalmic artery or aortic arch disease. Reduced ocular perfusion pressure causes chronic ischaemia of the retina, choroid and anterior segment. Retinal and anterior segment hypoxia stimulates release of vascular endothelial growth factor, driving neovascularisation of the iris, angle and retina that can progress to neovascular glaucoma. Ischaemia of the ciliary body reduces aqueous production, which can paradoxically keep intraocular pressure low despite angle neovascularisation. Persistent hypoperfusion leads to progressive retinal and optic nerve damage.
additionalDifferentials: Central retinal vein occlusion (non-ischaemic and ischaemic)
Giant cell arteritis with ocular ischaemia
Anterior segment or intraocular inflammation causing rubeosis
additionalInvestigations: Carotid Doppler ultrasonography, and where indicated CT or MR angiography, to assess carotid stenosis
Fluorescein angiography to demonstrate delayed arm-to-retina and arteriovenous transit and patchy choroidal filling
Gonioscopy to detect angle neovascularisation and intraocular pressure measurement
Dilated fundus examination for mid-peripheral haemorrhages and vascular changes
Systemic cardiovascular evaluation including blood pressure, glucose, lipids and cardiac assessment
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein if giant cell arteritis is a consideration
redFlags: Iris or angle neovascularisation heralding neovascular glaucoma
Critical carotid stenosis carrying a high risk of stroke
Rapidly progressive visual loss from worsening ischaemia
Systemic features suggesting giant cell arteritis in an older patient
reference.prognosis: The visual prognosis is generally guarded, particularly once neovascularisation or neovascular glaucoma develops, and the syndrome carries a substantial risk of stroke and cardiovascular death, so systemic vascular management is as important as ocular treatment.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the retinopathy as an ordinary central retinal vein occlusion and missing the underlying carotid disease
Overlooking the systemic (stroke and cardiac) mortality risk and failing to refer for vascular assessment
Being falsely reassured by a normal or low intraocular pressure despite florid angle neovascularisation
Not considering giant cell arteritis in an older patient with ocular ischaemia
Delaying panretinal photocoagulation or anti-VEGF until neovascular glaucoma is established
management: Treatment of the underlying carotid occlusive disease with carotid endarterectomy or stenting for significant stenosis, in conjunction with vascular surgery
Aggressive systemic vascular risk reduction with antiplatelet therapy, statins and control of hypertension, diabetes and smoking to reduce the high risk of stroke and cardiac death
Panretinal photocoagulation and intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy for iris, angle and retinal neovascularisation
Management of neovascular glaucoma with topical intraocular-pressure-lowering agents and, where needed, cyclodestructive or glaucoma drainage surgery
Intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy for associated macular oedema
Urgent multidisciplinary referral to stroke, vascular surgery and cardiology services alongside ophthalmology
Regular ophthalmic surveillance with gonioscopy and intraocular pressure monitoring to detect progressive neovascularisation early
